sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Prowler Sled Push is a full-body conditioning exercise performed by pushing a weighted sled across the floor.

It combines leg drive, core stability, and upper body bracing, making it an incredibly effective tool for building explosive power, strength-endurance, and cardiovascular fitness.

Because there is no eccentric phase, prowler pushes produce minimal muscle soreness while delivering a maximal training stimulus.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Builds explosive leg and hip power
- Excellent cardiovascular conditioning
- Trains the entire posterior chain
- Low impact on joints (no eccentric load)
- Minimal muscle soreness afterwards
- Scalable — adjust load and distance
- Boosts work capacity and GPP
- Strong mental toughness builder

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Quadriceps, Glutes, Hamstrings, Calves

Secondary: Core, Lower Back, Shoulders, Chest, Triceps (bracing)

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Load the Prowler sled with the desired amount of weight.
2. Adjust the handles to a comfortable height for pushing.
3. Stand behind the Prowler with your feet shoulder-width apart.
4. Bend at your hips and knees to lower your body into a squatting position.
5. Grip the handles with your hands at about chest height.
6. Keep your back straight and core braced.
7. Lean forward into the sled.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Push the Prowler sled forward by extending your hips and knees explosively.
2. Keep your back straight and maintain a strong core as you drive the sled forward.
3. Use powerful strides and maintain a brisk pace.
4. Continue pushing the sled for the desired distance or time.
5. Maintain good form throughout the entire push.
6. Keep a consistent and controlled pace.
7. When finished, carefully stop the sled and step away.
8. Rest as needed between sets.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Standing too upright — reduces leg drive
- Looking down instead of ahead
- Short, choppy strides
- Rounding the lower back
- Bending the elbows excessively
- Loading too much weight and sacrificing pace
- Holding breath throughout the effort
- Stopping abruptly without controlling the sled

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Prowler Sled
- Weight Plates
- Flat, smooth surface (turf, rubber, or concrete)
- Training shoes with good grip
- Optional: Gloves for hand comfort
- Clear lane of at least 10-20 metres

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Stance: Feet shoulder-width apart behind the sled.
2. Body Angle: Leaning forward at roughly 45 degrees.
3. Grip: Firm on the handles at chest height.
4. Arms: Extended, elbows mostly straight.
5. Back: Flat with a neutral spine.
6. Core: Braced hard throughout.
7. Head: Neutral, eyes looking slightly ahead.
8. Feet: Driving through the balls of the feet.

sections.heading: Progression Tips
sections.content:
1. Start light to learn the pushing mechanics.
2. Focus on powerful leg drive, not pace, at first.
3. Keep pushes short (10-20m) for power work.
4. Use longer distances for conditioning work.
5. Gradually increase weight once form is solid.
6. Vary grip heights — low for power, high for speed.
7. Alternate forward and backward sled work for balance.
8. Manage rest periods based on your goal.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Sled Drag: Pulled variation for posterior chain
- Reverse Sled Drag: Quad-focused backward pulling
- Farmer's Walk: Full-body loaded carry
- Battle Ropes: Cardiovascular conditioning
- Hill Sprints: Similar power/conditioning blend
- Yoke Carry: Heavy loaded locomotion

sections.heading: Conditioning Variations
sections.content:
Heavy Push: Short distance, maximum load — power focus
Light Push: Long distance, fast pace — conditioning focus
High Handle Push: More upright, speed biased
Low Handle Push: Lower body angle, strength biased
Sled Drag (Forwards/Backwards): Alternative stimulus
Sprint Intervals: Pure cardiovascular option

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Lower Back Issues: Use high handles and lighter loads
Knee Issues: Reduce load and shorten stride
Shoulder Issues: Keep arms extended and avoid excessive bracing
No Sled Available: Use a weight plate pushed on a towel or hill sprints
Limited Space: Focus on short, heavy pushes
Beginner: Start with bodyweight pace and very light load to learn the pattern
